subject: chemistry
title: Using materials (chemistry only)

concepts.def: The destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment. It is a chemical change, not simply wear, and it is not confined to metals.
The corrosion of iron. It is one example of corrosion, and both air and water must be present for it to happen.
A layer applied to a metal that keeps air and water away from the surface, for example grease, paint or an electroplated layer of another metal.
Using electricity to deposit a thin layer of one metal onto the surface of another, used here as a way of applying a protective barrier.
The thin layer of oxide that forms on the surface of aluminium and protects the metal underneath from further corrosion.
Protecting a metal by putting it in contact with a more reactive metal, which corrodes in its place.
Coating iron or steel with zinc. The zinc acts as a barrier and, because it is more reactive than iron, also gives sacrificial protection.

concepts.term: Fair test in a rusting experiment
concepts.def: Setting up tubes that differ in only one factor - air present or absent, water present or absent - so that any difference in rusting can be traced to that one factor.
A substance such as anhydrous calcium chloride that removes water vapour, used to give a nail air without water.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements. Most metals in everyday use are alloys because the mixture has more useful properties than the pure metal.
An alloy of copper and tin, used for statues, ornaments and bells.
An alloy of copper and zinc, used for musical instruments, door fittings and taps.
Gold mixed with silver, copper and zinc, which is harder and cheaper than pure gold.
The unit used for the proportion of gold in an alloy. 24 carat is 100% gold and 18 carat is 75% gold.
An alloy of iron containing specific amounts of carbon and, in some steels, other metals.
Steel with a higher proportion of carbon. It is strong but brittle, so it is used for cutting tools and blades.
Steel with a lower proportion of carbon. It is softer and more easily shaped, so it is used for car bodies and sheeting.
Steel containing chromium and nickel. It is hard and resistant to corrosion, so it is used for cutlery, sinks and surgical tools.
An alloy of aluminium. Aluminium alloys are low density, so they are used for aircraft bodies and bicycle frames.
The glass in ordinary use, made by heating a mixture of sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.
Glass made from sand and boron trioxide. It melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.
A material such as pottery or brick, made by shaping wet clay and then heating it in a furnace.
The small molecule from which a polymer is built. Ethene is the monomer for poly(ethene).
Low density poly(ethene), made from ethene under one set of conditions with one catalyst. It is flexible and used for bags and bottles.
High density poly(ethene), made from the same monomer, ethene, but with a different catalyst and different conditions. It is stiffer and stronger.
A polymer made of separate tangled chains held to each other only by weak forces, so it melts when heated and can be reshaped.
A polymer whose chains are joined by cross-links. It does not melt when heated, so it keeps its shape at high temperature.
Strong bonds joining one polymer chain to another, which stop the chains moving past each other on heating.
A material made of two materials: a matrix or binder surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of a second material.
The material in a composite that surrounds and holds the reinforcement, for example the cement in concrete.
The fibres or fragments held inside the matrix of a composite, for example the gravel in concrete or the glass fibres in fibreglass.
Mass per unit volume. A low density material has a small mass for its size, which is why aluminium alloys suit aircraft.

mcqs.q: What is meant by corrosion?
options: The destruction of materials by chemical reactions with the environment
Damage suffered only by metals, caused by oxygen in the air
The rusting of iron that has been left outside in the wet
The wearing away of a surface by scratching, rubbing and use
mcqs.explain: This is the specification definition: corrosion is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment.

mcqs.q: Which conditions are necessary for iron to rust?
options: Water alone; the air around the iron plays no part in it
Both air and water in contact with the iron surface
Air alone, since rust is simply an oxide of iron
Salt water only, as pure water cannot rust iron
mcqs.explain: The specification states that both air and water are necessary for iron to rust.

mcqs.q: A nail is put in a tube of water that has been boiled and then covered with a layer of oil. After a week the nail has not rusted. What does this show?
options: The layer of oil is what stopped the nail rusting here
Rusting needs only air, so the water was never needed
Water on its own cannot rust iron, so air is needed
A week is not long enough for rusting to be seen
mcqs.explain: Boiling drives dissolved air out and the oil stops it returning. The nail has water but no air and does not rust, so air is necessary as well.

mcqs.q: A nail is sealed in a tube of air with anhydrous calcium chloride at the bottom. After a week it has not rusted. What does this show?
options: Calcium chloride is a chemical that prevents rust
Air plays no part in the rusting of iron at all
Sealing up the tube is what kept the nail shiny here
Dry air cannot rust iron, so water is needed
mcqs.explain: The calcium chloride removes water vapour, so the nail has air but no water. It does not rust, so water is necessary as well.

mcqs.q: Which method prevents corrosion by acting as a barrier?
options: Painting the surface so that air and water cannot reach the metal
Bolting blocks of magnesium along the outside of the pipe
Heating the metal strongly to harden its outside layer
Mixing carbon into the metal to turn it into an alloy
mcqs.explain: Greasing, painting and electroplating are the barrier methods named by the specification; they keep air and water off the surface.

mcqs.q: Aluminium is a reactive metal, yet aluminium window frames do not corrode away. Why not?
options: Aluminium is unreactive, so nothing in the air can attack it
An oxide coating forms that protects the metal underneath
Its oxide flakes away, leaving fresh clean metal behind
Frames are always painted before they are fitted
mcqs.explain: Aluminium has an oxide coating that protects the metal from further corrosion.

mcqs.q: Iron sheets are galvanised. What does this mean?
options: They are coated with tin, a metal that resists corrosion
They are dipped in acid to clean them before painting
They are coated with zinc, which is more reactive
They are melted together with zinc as an alloy
mcqs.explain: Galvanising is coating iron with zinc, a more reactive metal that gives sacrificial protection.

mcqs.q: A galvanised bucket is scratched right through to the iron. Why does the iron still not rust?
options: The zinc melts and seals the scratch up again
The iron corrodes first and so protects the zinc
The scratch is too narrow for water to get into
The zinc corrodes away in place of the iron
mcqs.explain: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes instead: sacrificial protection works even where the coating is broken.

mcqs.q: Blocks of metal are bolted to a steel ship's hull to give sacrificial protection. Which metal should be used?
options: Magnesium, as it is more reactive than iron and corrodes first
Copper, because it is less reactive and resists corrosion
Tin, because it sits below iron and will not be eaten away
Lead, because it is dense and very heavy for its size
mcqs.explain: Sacrificial protection needs a metal above iron in the reactivity series, so it reacts in the iron's place.

mcqs.q: Why are most metals in everyday use alloys rather than pure metals?
options: Alloys are compounds, so they cannot react with air at all
The mixture has properties, like hardness, that suit the job
Mixing metals always makes them much softer and easier to bend
Pure metals cost far too much to make in large amounts
mcqs.explain: Most metals in everyday use are alloys because mixing gives more useful properties than the pure metal has.

mcqs.q: Which statement about bronze is correct?
options: It is copper mixed with zinc in fixed amounts
It is a compound formed from copper and tin
It is an alloy of copper mixed with tin
It is a pure metal mined as bronze ore
mcqs.explain: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin.

mcqs.q: Brass is used for musical instruments and door fittings. What is brass?
options: A mixture of copper and pure tin
A compound of copper and zinc
Iron with a thin copper coating
A mixture of copper and zinc
mcqs.explain: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, which is why it is used for instruments and fittings.

mcqs.q: Gold used as jewellery is usually an alloy. Which metals is the gold usually mixed with?
options: The gold is mixed with silver, copper and zinc
Nothing else, since jewellery gold is pure
Iron and carbon, added to harden the gold
A compound of gold, silver, copper and zinc
mcqs.explain: Gold used as jewellery is usually an alloy with silver, copper and zinc.

mcqs.q: A ring is stamped 18 carat. What does this tell you about the ring?
options: It contains 18% gold and 82% of other metals
It is 75% gold, because 24 carat means pure gold
It is pure gold and it weighs 18 carats on a balance
It has 18 parts of gold to 24 parts of other metal
mcqs.explain: Carats are measured out of 24, so 18 carat is 18/24, which is 75% gold.

mcqs.q: How does high carbon steel differ from low carbon steel?
options: High carbon steel is soft and easy to shape; low carbon steel is brittle
High carbon steel resists corrosion; low carbon steel rusts very fast
High carbon steel is strong but brittle; low carbon steel is softer
High carbon steel is a pure metal; low carbon steel is an alloy
mcqs.explain: High carbon steel is strong but brittle, while low carbon steel is softer and more easily shaped.

mcqs.q: Why is stainless steel chosen for cutlery and sinks?
options: It is pure iron, so there is nothing to rust
It has extra carbon in it, which stops any rust
It is soft, so it can be pressed into thin sheets
It is hard and it resists corrosion well
mcqs.explain: Steels containing chromium and nickel are hard and resistant to corrosion.

mcqs.q: Aluminium alloys are used for the bodies of aircraft. Which property makes them suitable?
options: They are low density, so a given volume of them weighs less
They are the strongest metals known, so they never bend
They have a low mass whatever the size of the part
They melt easily, so parts can be cast into shape
mcqs.explain: Aluminium alloys are low density, so an aircraft body made from them is lighter to lift.

mcqs.q: Duralumin is an alloy of aluminium with copper and magnesium. Its density is 2.8 g/cm3 and it is harder than pure aluminium. A titanium alloy has a density of 4.5 g/cm3 and is harder than duralumin. Which is the better choice for a lightweight bicycle frame that must not bend?
options: Titanium alloy, because it is the harder of the two
Duralumin, because it is far less dense and still hard
Titanium alloy, because a denser metal is always stronger
Pure aluminium, because it is the softest of them all
mcqs.explain: The frame must be light, and 2.8 g/cm3 is well below 4.5 g/cm3, while duralumin is still harder than pure aluminium.

mcqs.q: Soda-lime glass is made by heating a mixture of which substances?
options: Sand with boron trioxide, heated strongly
Sand on its own, melted in a hot furnace
Sand, sodium carbonate and limestone
Clay, limestone and sodium chloride
mcqs.explain: Most of the glass we use is soda-lime glass, made by heating a mixture of sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.

mcqs.q: How does borosilicate glass differ from soda-lime glass?
options: It melts at a much lower temperature
It is made from sand and limestone
It cannot be melted at all once set
It melts at a higher temperature
mcqs.explain: Borosilicate glass, made from sand and boron trioxide, melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.

mcqs.q: How are clay ceramics such as bricks and pottery made?
options: Wet clay is shaped and then heated in a furnace
Clay is melted and poured into a cold mould
Dry clay powder is pressed and left to set
Clay is mixed with sand and melted down
mcqs.explain: Clay ceramics, including pottery and bricks, are made by shaping wet clay and then heating in a furnace.

mcqs.q: LD and HD poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene. Why do they have different properties?
options: They are built from two different monomers
A different catalyst and conditions are used
HD poly(ethene) is pressed hard after it is made
The HD chains contain a second element
mcqs.explain: The properties of polymers depend on the monomer and on the conditions under which they are made, so the same ethene gives two different materials.

mcqs.q: Why do thermosoftening polymers melt when they are heated?
options: The strong covalent bonds along the chains break
The cross-links joining the chains snap apart
Separate chains are held only by weak forces
The polymer is a liquid that was frozen
mcqs.explain: The chains are separate and tangled, with only weak forces between them, so they slide apart when heated.

mcqs.q: Why do thermosetting polymers keep their shape when they are heated?
options: They only melt above about a thousand degrees
Their chains are tangled but are not joined up
They contain no carbon that could be melted
Cross-links join the chains to each other
mcqs.explain: The chains in a thermosetting polymer are joined by cross-links, so they cannot slide apart and the polymer does not melt.

mcqs.q: Most composites are made of two materials. How are those two materials arranged?
options: A matrix surrounds and binds together fibres or fragments
Two materials are melted into a single new substance
Fibres surround the matrix and hold it firmly in place
Two elements are joined chemically to give a compound
mcqs.explain: Most composites are made of a matrix or binder surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of the reinforcement.

mcqs.q: Which of these materials is a composite?
options: Brass, which is copper mixed with zinc
Concrete, gravel held together by cement
Poly(ethene), made from many ethene units
Soda-lime glass, made by melting sand
mcqs.explain: Concrete is a composite: cement is the matrix and the gravel is the reinforcement.

mcqs.q: A table gives: aluminium alloy, density 2.7 g/cm3, does not shatter; soda-lime glass, density 2.5 g/cm3, shatters when dropped; carbon fibre composite, density 1.6 g/cm3, does not shatter. Which material is lightest for a given volume and survives being dropped?
options: Soda-lime glass, since glass is the lightest here
Aluminium alloy, since a metal can never break
The carbon fibre composite, the least dense
Aluminium alloy, as it is the densest one
mcqs.explain: At 1.6 g/cm3 it is the least dense of the three, and the table says it does not shatter.

mcqs.q: A saucepan handle must not soften on the hot hob and must not conduct heat well. Which material is most suitable?
options: A thermosoftening polymer
A toughened soda-lime glass
A hard-wearing steel alloy
A thermosetting polymer
mcqs.explain: Thermosetting polymers do not melt when heated and, being polymers, are poor conductors of heat.

mcqs.q: Which object is most likely to be made from bronze?
options: A church bell cast in one piece
A trumpet played in a school band
A knife blade that stays sharp
A drinks can pressed from thin sheet
mcqs.explain: Bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, is used for bells, statues and ornaments.

mcqs.q: What is high carbon steel used for?
options: Car body panels and sheeting
Cutlery and kitchen sinks
Cutting tools and sharp blades
Aeroplane bodies and frames
mcqs.explain: High carbon steel is strong but brittle, which suits cutting tools and blades.
